The Black-billed amazon (Amazona agilis), a medium-sized parrot endemic to Jamaica, is one of the smaller members of the genus. Hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] after a developmental period averaging 27 days [ab = 27 days], a duration that aligns closely with that of other Caribbean Amazona species. At the moment of hatching, these altricial nestlings typically exhibit a wet weight of approximately 14 grams [Wwb = approximately 14 grams], representing a modest initial mass that demands intensive parental provisioning. This neonatal body mass is considerably less than that of older nestlings, as growth rates are rapid during the first weeks of life. The relatively short incubation period and small hatchling size may be adaptive responses to the seasonal and climatic constraints of the island’s montane forests, where these parrots predominantly reside. Field records indicate that the timing of hatching is closely synchronized with peak fruit availability, ensuring a steady supply of food for the growing chick.

As the nestling develops, it undergoes a marked transformation in body mass and feathering. By the time the chick approaches the point of fledging, its wet weight has increased substantially, ultimately reaching an adult body mass of around 212.25 grams [Wwi = around 212.25 grams]. This maximum recorded value, consistent with the 178–220 gram range reported in the literature (CollBoes2020), reflects the species’ relatively small size compared to larger Amazonian congeners. Throughout the nestling phase, the chick is reliant on regurgitated food from both parents, a period during which mass gain is steep and the development of flight feathers proceeds rapidly. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]), the time since birth at fledging is approximately 56 days [tx = approximately 56 days]. This milestone marks the young bird’s first flight and departure from the nest cavity, though post-fledging dependence on parental care often extends for several additional weeks while the juvenile hones its foraging skills.

The onset of reproductive maturity in Amazona agilis is a comparatively slow process, typical of long-lived parrots with low annual fecundity. Field studies have indicated that, under the same thermal regime of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the time since birth at puberty is reached at about 168 days [tp = about 168 days], although this early physiological capability does not translate into immediate breeding. In this species, the age at first successful reproduction is considerably later, reflecting the need for complex social learning and territory establishment. The first brood is typically produced at an age of 3 years after hatching [tR = 3 years after hatching], a delay that is common among long-lived psittacids that invest heavily in each nesting attempt at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This deferred reproduction allows young adults to acquire essential foraging experience and secure stable nest cavities, which are often a limiting resource in Jamaica’s fragmented forests. The combination of a modest clutch size and delayed breeding underscores a conservative life-history strategy.

Reproductive output in this species is characterized by a small clutch, with females typically laying 2.9 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2.9 eggs per clutch]. This value represents the maximum recorded fecundity per nesting event and is relatively low compared to some mainland parrots, reflecting the constraints of an island environment where resources are unpredictable. The frequency with which these clutches are produced is also limited; available data suggest that breeding pairs generally manage only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. The combination of a modest clutch size and an annual single-brood strategy yields a correspondingly low annual reproductive rate, a pattern consistent with many K-selected tropical birds. The energetic demands of incubation and chick rearing are substantial, and the energy budgets of breeding adults are tightly constrained by the availability of native fruits and seeds. The species' comparatively slow life-history pace is also reflected in its prolonged developmental phases and extended lifespan.

This maximum longevity, recorded at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], places the Black-billed amazon among the longer-lived members of its genus and is consistent with the typical survival patterns of large-bodied parrots that experience low adult mortality rates. Such an extended lifespan allows ample opportunity for repeated reproductive attempts, potentially balancing the modest annual fecundity over a lifetime. The species’ ability to persist for several decades is likely linked to its dietary flexibility, reliance on stable cavity roosts, and low predation pressure on the island. Moreover, the relatively slow pace of somatic development and the deferred onset of reproduction are hallmarks of a life-history trajectory shaped by ecological stability and resource limitation. These demographic characteristics make the Black-billed amazon particularly vulnerable to habitat loss and any increase in adult mortality, as the population’s growth rate depends heavily on the survival of long-lived, breeding adults.
